query: cryptocurrency mining GPU and ASIC demand

output.content:
**Bottom line:** cryptocurrency-mining hardware demand is now overwhelmingly an **ASIC replacement-and-expansion cycle**, while GPU mining is a much smaller, volatile niche tied to alternative proof-of-work coins rather than a broad driver of graphics-card sales. [[1]] [[2]]

**ASIC demand—structurally strong, but economically selective.** Bitcoin requires purpose-built SHA-256 ASICs rather than GPUs, and industrial operators are continually replacing older fleets with more efficient hardware as network difficulty rises and post-halving rewards are compressed. [[3]] [[4]] Bitcoin’s block subsidy has been 3.125 BTC since the April 2024 halving, so miners’ returns depend heavily on BTC price, transaction fees, electricity cost, uptime, and the network’s aggregate hashrate. [[4]] The market has therefore shifted toward high-efficiency equipment and operators with low-cost power, rather than indiscriminate fleet growth. [[5]] [[6]]

**Evidence of current ASIC purchasing and deployment demand is tangible.** Canaan reported Q4 2025 product revenue of $164.9 million, up 124.5% year over year, principally due to a landmark order for more than 50,000 A15 Pro miners; it also sold 36.5 EH/s of computing power in the quarter, up 40.7% year over year. [[7]] Bitdeer generated $108.3 million of 2025 revenue from SEALMINER and accessory sales while expanding mining-rig assets to $620.7 million from $67.3 million, reflecting both external sales and internal deployment. [[8]] Bitdeer also reached 41.2 EH/s of self-mining hashrate by late October 2025 and began mass production of its SEALMINER A3 series, with early SEAL04 samples demonstrating 6–7 J/TH efficiency. [[9]]

**The key ASIC demand driver is efficiency, not simply coin-price optimism.** Electricity represents more than 80% of a typical miner’s cash operating cost, making lower joules-per-terahash directly valuable to mining margins and accelerating retirement of older machines. [[6]] As an illustration of the technology step-up, Bitmain’s S21 XP Hyd. was marketed at 473 TH/s and 12 J/TH, while newer-generation equipment has pushed the industry toward sub-15 J/TH economics. [[10]] [[5]] In July 2026 conditions cited by one industry source, an S21 XP could break even around $0.088/kWh, whereas older S19-class equipment required power below roughly $0.055/kWh, highlighting why demand is concentrated in efficient new units and low-cost-power sites. [[5]]

**ASIC demand risks:** higher hashrate and difficulty can erode returns even if Bitcoin’s price is stable, while a sharp BTC-price decline, lower transaction fees, power-price inflation, delivery delays, trade restrictions, or financing constraints can postpone miner orders. [[11]] [[1]] Hardware pricing is also cyclical: Bitmain’s cited S21 XP Hyd. price fell from $30.6/TH at launch in 2024 to $21.5/TH for a Q4 2025 batch, illustrating that manufacturer unit volumes can rise while realized pricing and margins remain under pressure. [[10]] ASIC suppliers are relatively concentrated, with one Cambridge-based estimate assigning approximately 82% share to Bitmain, 15% to MicroBT, and 2% to Canaan in 2025, although exact shares vary by source and period. [[6]]

**GPU demand—structurally weaker than the pre-2022 cycle.** Ethereum’s September 15, 2022 Merge transitioned Ethereum to proof-of-stake, eliminated energy-intensive mining on Ethereum Mainnet, and reduced the network’s energy consumption by approximately 99.95%. [[2]] Because Ethereum had been the dominant GPU-mining workload, its transition removed the largest broad-based source of crypto-related demand for consumer GPUs. [[1]] [[12]] NVIDIA itself states in its FY2026 10-K that crypto-market volatility, policy, verification-method changes, and the Ethereum 2.0 Merge have affected—and may continue to affect—mining-related demand for its products. [[1]]

**What remains for GPUs is a fragmented altcoin market.** GPUs retain an advantage where algorithm flexibility matters, supporting proof-of-work networks such as Ethereum Classic, Ravencoin, Ergo, Flux, and certain other smaller coins, but profitability is highly sensitive to token prices, difficulty, electricity rates, and competition from specialized machines. [[3]] [[12]] ASIC encroachment has further weakened GPU demand in some former GPU-oriented algorithms, including Kaspa, so GPU mining should be viewed as opportunistic demand rather than a dependable volume catalyst for NVIDIA or AMD. [[13]] [[14]]

**Investment implication:** ASIC vendors, foundries, power-infrastructure providers, cooling suppliers, and vertically integrated public miners have the clearer crypto-mining exposure, but their revenue outlook should be modeled against hashprice, power cost, fleet efficiency, and financing availability rather than BTC price alone. [[5]] [[11]] For GPU vendors, crypto mining is now primarily an upside or downside swing factor in channel inventory and used-card supply, not the core demand thesis it was during the Ethereum proof-of-work era. [[1]] [[2]]
